source.title: A CXL Memory Rack for Multi-Turn LLM Serving
source.summary: Long-context, multi-turn, and agentic LLM workloads increasingly reuse previously processed context, making KV-cache reuse essential for reducing redundant computation. However, this reuse shifts the bottleneck to the memory tier that stores and serves reusable KV states at cluster scale. GPU HBM and host DRAM are too costly to scale to TB-scale shared context capacity, motivating remote tiers built from lower-cost, higher-capacity media. This paper presents HyMCache, a CXL memory rack for multi-turn LLM serving. We build the memory rack using cost-efficient CXL-hybrid memory (CXL-HM), which combines a small amount of in-device DRAM with large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface. By exploiting the read-dominant, predictable, and append-only nature of multi-turn KV-cache access, HyMCache rethinks DRAM management within CXL-HM to efficiently support TB-scale SSD-backed KV reuse. It uses request-level prefix prefetching and opportunistic write buffering to stage latency-critical reads in device DRAM, enabling DRAM-scale KV-cache efficiency at SSD-level cost. We evaluate HyMCache on a real CXL-HM prototype under both single-aggregator and PD-disaggregated serving configurations. Under the same DRAM budget, HyMCache outperforms local LMCache by 3.0x in single-node serving and 1.45x in PD-disaggregated serving. Compared with 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake, HyMCache incurs about 30% lower performance but uses 16x less DRAM.

previous_facts.problem: Multi-turn LLM serving requires TB-scale shared KV-cache capacity to reuse context across turns and sessions, but GPU HBM and host DRAM are too costly to scale to this level. Storage-backed tiers provide capacity but require software staging overhead. Pure DRAM-based CXL memory pools provide low latency but remain expensive at multi-TB scale.
previous_facts.mechanism: HyMCache builds a remote memory rack using CXL-hybrid memory (CXL-HM), which combines small in-device DRAM with large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL.mem interface. It exploits read-dominant, predictable, and append-only KV-cache access patterns with request-level prefix prefetching and opportunistic write buffering to stage latency-critical reads in device DRAM, enabling DRAM-scale efficiency at SSD-level cost.

previous_facts.evaluation_context: Real CXL-HM prototype evaluation under two configurations: (1) single-aggregator serving, and (2) Prefill-Decode (PD) disaggregated serving with 64 GB per worker (256 GB total). Uses RDMA-capable network (100-400 Gbps) for remote memory access. Leverages vLLM serving engine with PagedAttention and Dynamo distributed framework with NIXL for P-D KV transfer.
previous_facts.limitations: Evidence pack covers only abstract/intro/background; exact workload details, model specifications, dataset characteristics, request traces, and full evaluation metrics are in unread sections. Performance claims in abstract (3.0x, 1.45x, 30% gap) lack concrete baseline conditions and metric definitions visible in this excerpt. Cost estimates are rough projections for FPGA prototypes, not production pricing. CXL-HM internal cache management policies (beyond LRU being insufficient) are not detailed in visible text.
previous_facts.project_relevance: This source addresses KV-cache memory tiering for multi-turn LLM serving, which is highly relevant to cross-region cache sharing questions. The CXL-HM approach explores remote memory access over RDMA networks, which directly relates to WAN RTT and bandwidth considerations for KV cache transport. The 16x DRAM reduction versus 30% performance trade-off quantifies a key cost-performance decision point relevant to cross-region cache economics. Request-level prefix prefetching for predictable, append-only access patterns could inform compression and prefill strategies for cross-domain transfer. However, this paper focuses on intra-datacenter CXL/RDMA memory tiers rather than true WAN cross-region deployment; actual cross-region WAN latency (tens of ms) would be orders of magnitude higher than the CXL/RDMA latencies discussed (600-750 ns for switch fabrics).
